segments.text: They found that most of them were neutral, but nine killed cancer cells and one took tadpole position.

segments.text: E. americana, a bacterium naturally occurring in the gut of Japanese tree frogs.

segments.speaker: Speaker 47
segments.text: When the team injected E. americana into the bloodstream of mice with colorectal tumors, the tumors' own leaky blood vessels let the bacteria slip out of circulation and into the tumor site itself.

segments.speaker: Speaker 47
segments.text: There, because the tumor produces a protein called CD47, which suppresses local immune defenses and helps the tumor go unnoticed, it also meant that the bacteria could evade the body's immune response and establish a colony undisturbed.

segments.text: Neutrophils arrived first, engulfing and destroying that bacteria directly while also attacking cancer cells that were caught in the crossfire.

segments.speaker: Speaker 47
segments.text: Drawn in by the same infection alarm, T-cells and B-cells then flooded in behind them, releasing inflammatory signals and helping the body spot the tumor, bind to it, and destroy it.
